title: The Best Withdrawal Strategies for Minimizing Taxes in Retirement
description: Sequential vs. Proportional withdrawals to extend portfolio life.
content:
Accumulating wealth is only half the battle; decumulating it efficiently is the other half. If you have money in Taxable, Tax-Deferred (Traditional), and Tax-Free (Roth) accounts, the order in which you withdraw funds determines how long your money lasts. A poor strategy can trigger unnecessary taxes, higher Medicare premiums, and Social Security taxation. The optimal strategy smooths your tax bracket over 30 years, paying the minimum legal tax rate on every dollar spent.

Key Takeaways

  • The Standard Strategy (Sequential): Withdraw Taxable first, then Traditional, then Roth. This allows tax-advantaged money to grow longest, but can create massive 'Tax Bombs' (RMDs) in your 70s.
  • The Modern Strategy (Proportional): Withdraw from all three buckets annually to 'fill up' low tax brackets (e.g., the 12% bracket) without spilling over. This smooths tax liability.
  • Roth Conversions: Use 'Low Income Years' (early retirement before Social Security) to convert Traditional funds to Roth up to the top of your tax bracket. This lowers future RMDs.
  • Capital Gains Harvesting: If your income is low enough (<$94k married), sell taxable stocks to realize gains at 0% tax rate. This is free money.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US tax code has 'Tax Torpedoes' where earning $1 extra income triggers tax on 85% of your Social Security. Strategic withdrawal planning navigates around these cliffs to preserve wealth.

The Withdrawal Hierarchy

Optimize your AGI (Adjusted Gross Income) annually.

Priority 1: RMDs (Mandatory)

Once you hit age 73, you must take Required Minimum Distributions from Traditional accounts. This fills your tax bracket 'floor' first.

Priority 2: Taxable Brokerage (0% / 15% Gains)

Sell assets here next.
Goal: Stay under the ~$94k (married) income limit to pay 0% Capital Gains Tax. This is the most efficient money you have.

Priority 3: Traditional IRA (Top-Up)

Withdraw enough to fill the 12% Ordinary Income bracket (up to ~$94k).
Goal: Don't spill into the 22% bracket unnecessarily.

Priority 4: Roth IRA (The Cap)

If you need more cash for a big purchase (new car), pull it from Roth.
Why? It doesn't count as taxable income, so it won't push you into a higher bracket or trigger Medicare surcharges (IRMAA).

Tactical Planning

  1. The Gap Years (60-70): You have stopped working but haven't claimed Social Security. Your income is $0. This is the prime time for massive Roth Conversions to 'fill' the 12% or 22% bracket at a discount.
  2. Specific ID Selling: In your taxable account, sell 'High Cost' shares first (shares you bought recently or at high prices). This minimizes the realized gain and tax bill.
  3. Donor Advised Fund: If you give to charity, donate appreciated stock directly from your taxable account to avoid capital gains tax entirely.
  4. HSA as Super-Roth: Save the HSA for last. It can pay Medicare premiums tax-free, effectively making it better than a Roth in late life.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need software for this?

Yes. The math of interacting tax brackets, Social Security taxation, and ACA subsidies is complex. Tools like NewRetirement or Pralana Gold are worth the subscription.

What is IRMAA?

Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount. If you withdraw too much (AGI > $206k married), your Medicare premiums triple. Use Roth withdrawals to stay under this cliff.

Should I spend Roth last?

Usually yes. Tax-free compounding becomes more powerful the longer it runs. It is also the best asset to leave to heirs (no tax bomb for them).
